chapter: Blanton, Los Angeles and Art Tatum
title: First reaction to bebop; recording with Dizzy Gillespie and Charlie Parker
summary: Stewart went along with bebop and was hired for record sessions with Gillespie and Parker (Hot House), crediting his Tatum experience for his ease with it.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Now, around that time too the be-bop style was beginning to develop.
Yes.
How did -- how did that music strike you
Well, I thought it was something different, and I went right along with it because I did play a few gigs with a couple of the be-boppers, Dizzy and Charlie. In fact I recorded with Dizzy and Charlie.
Did you play with --
(Singing.)
-- Hot House, did you play with 'Hot House'?
Yes, he was on there.
And I think you played 'Dizzy Atmosphere.' Were you on 'Dizzy Atmosphere'?
No, I didn't.
'Hot House' was 'All the Things You Are.' *
All the Things You Are, I think. I even played 'Peanuts' (phonetic).
'Saltines,' right.
And quite a few.
Did 'Nuff' 'Shaving Off', did you --
'Nuff' 'Shaving Off', I don't think I was on that.
And that's right, Sid Catlett was on (inaudible), right?
Sid Catlett did quite a few.
Sid Catlett was on bass. And I think Clyde Hart or somebody was playing piano. & DRUMS!
* 'What Is This Thing Called Love' harmony.
Yeah.
Now, how did the sessions go when you played? How -- did you -- they hired you -- did you play with them on any club dates?
No. They just hired me for the record session.
Uh-huh. Did -- so you -- did you like the style when you first heard it?
Oh, yes, I say, well, to myself, this is different. And I've always searched for new sounds and what have you, and that was quite a -- be-bop was quite a sound, changes and what have you, rhythm.
Well, that was when the guys started playing more complex harmonies, started using more substitutions and more diminished kinds of things.
Oh, yes.
And like -- but -- so did you think that your working with Tatum made it easier for you to grasp the new styles than if you hadn't played with him?
Right. Working with him, I feel that that had a lot to do with my being able to fall right in with that be-bop craze or whatever you want to call it.
